name: PT Paragon Karya Perkasa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Paragon Karya Perkasa — a coal newcomer priced for flawless execution
frontmatter.summary: PKPK has pivoted from loss-making construction to coal mining and captive barging, and now trades on a multiple usually reserved for growth companies. On the approved annual quota, the last actual realised price and margins, both our DCF and the coal-peer multiple sit far below the market. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The group is now a coal miner and barge operator, not a contractor; pooling the shipping business restated history and left a related-party purchase payable that behaves like debt.

Sales sit below the approved quota today and the base case stops at that quota; the ramp to the road's capacity is a permit the state has not granted, so it sits outside every scenario we run, the bull included.

The mine's life to FY2041E depends on the first ten-year extension of a licence that expires in 2031; we assume it, weight it at ninety per cent, and show that a refusal would leave the flows before 2032 short of the debt and the minorities.
Margins are held at the last actual, not improved; shipping has been squeezed by fuel and we assume no recovery without evidence.
The price discounts growth and margins several steps beyond anything the company has delivered, and our target implies a substantial de-rating.
Governance is the swing factor, with control held by one family and both acquisitions struck with related parties.

catalysts.event: Extraordinary shareholder meeting on the one-for-ten stock split and the second shipping tranche
FY2026 audited results, first full year of consolidated shipping
Work plan and budget production quota for 2027

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Paragon Karya Perkasa at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp1,702, a total return of -72.2% against the last traded price of Rp6,125 [S0]. The company is no longer the small construction contractor that the data pack's history describes: in 2024 it bought a coal miner from its controlling shareholder, and in 2026 it pooled in a coal-transport operator owned by parties connected to the same group. Coal sales and shipping now produce almost all of revenue [S3][S2].

The disagreement with the market is not about whether PKPK has a business. It does: a licensed mine with a defined reserve, an owned hauling road, and a fleet of barges and tugs. The disagreement is about what that business can earn, and how much of it the company is permitted to sell. Our base case sells the 3.0 Mt quota the Ministry approved for 2026, which the company reaches in FY2028E and holds - because that is the one volume the state has granted. It is not the 5.0 Mtpa the owned hauling road can carry, and it is worth saying plainly which way this went: the previous revision assumed a ramp to the road's capacity, and the evidence does not support it. The company delivered the whole of its RKAB target in FY2025, so the quota is the volume the operator actually delivers; a higher quota is an annual decision it does not yet hold [S2][S4]. The realised price is held flat in real terms and costs and capex at the last actual [S3][S2]. That produces revenue of IDR2,925.0bn in the first step-up year and EBITDA of IDR771.9bn [S0]. On the bridge-consistent enterprise value the shares trade at eleven point nine times that EBITDA and 24.4x forward earnings [S0]. The DCF that we lead with values the equity at Rp1,439 per share on the pre-split count, one tenth of that once the one-for-ten split trades in late December 2026 [S6]. The independent KJPP appraisal of 31 July 2026 put the whole equity at Rp4,907 a share; the valuation section explains why we do not adopt it [S6].

Three things move the value. First, the quota: every tonne above the approved quota is a permit the company has to obtain year by year, and no scenario we run assumes one [S4]. Second, the licence term: the IUP-OP expires on 20 July 2031 and the licence provides for two extensions, so over half of the enterprise value sits after the expiry date and is worth what the first extension is worth [S3]. Third, the balance sheet: a purchase payable to a fellow shareholder sits ahead of equity and is deducted as debt [S3].

What does the market believe? Running our model backwards, the traded price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 64.4% against our 50.0% [S0]. That is not a one-year solve: the engine applies the same fourteen-point addition to revenue growth in every forecast year, so the path carries revenue to several times our terminal size by FY2041E - a volume path the quota does not support and a licence extension we have already weighted at ninety per cent. Our view is that the shares are priced for the best case; the base case is a good mine in a bad industry.

A note on how to read this name. Indonesian coal licences are production permits with a fixed term
and a royalty schedule set by government regulation; the royalty is levied on the reference price,
not on the company's own invoice, so a producer selling at a discount to the reference still pays
royalty on the higher number. The financial statements of Indonesian listed companies use the direct
cash-flow method, which means the depreciation charge does not appear as a single line and data
vendors frequently report a fraction of it. Where the vendor figure and the filing disagree, this
report uses the filing.

PKPK operates two segments and a residual: coal mining, coal logistics, and the construction business from which it came. In FY2025 the mining segment produced IDR732.4bn of revenue against IDR749.4bn consolidated, with construction contributing the difference [S2]. After the pooling of the shipping entity the mix widened sharply: in the nine months to September 2026 coal sales were IDR888.7bn and shipping services IDR556.5bn, with the residual construction business a small remainder [S3].

Mining sits in PT Tri Oetama Persada (TOP), held through PT Bhakti Harapan Sejahtera (BHS), which PKPK owns almost wholly and which in turn holds seven tenths of TOP, leaving an effective interest just under seventy per cent [S2][S3]. TOP began commercial operations in September 2024 [S2]. It holds an IUP production licence over 10,000 hectares in Kapuas regency, Central Kalimantan, granted for twenty years from July 2011 and extendable twice [S3]. The independent report of September 2023 records proved reserves of 50.0 Mt and probable reserves of 14.0 Mt, with total measured, indicated and inferred resources of 424 Mt [S3].

Output was about 1.1 Mt in FY2025 [S2]. The Ministry approved a work plan and budget for 2026 with a production quota of 3 Mt for TOP [S4]. The company has prioritised low-stripping areas at a ratio of 3.0 [S2], owns roughly 60 km of hauling road capable of supporting 5.0 Mt a year, and describes that road as its principal operational advantage because it removes dependence on third-party hauliers for the mine-to-barge leg [S2].

Logistics is PT Deli Pratama Angkutan Laut (DPAL), a vessel operator consolidated following the purchase of a stake from Resources Global Development in the first half of 2026 and due to rise to almost full ownership under the second tranche announced in November 2026, which would bring IDR556.5bn of shipping revenue and a fleet of sixty-seven bulk carriers, barges and tugs into wholly owned territory [S3][S6]. The purchase price of the second tranche was fixed in the announcement and is to be financed with third-party facilities [S6].

The customer base is narrow. Two buyers accounted for more than a fifth of consolidated revenue in the first nine months of 2026, the largest being PT Prima Jaya Coaltrade at IDR217.7bn [S3]. Related-party revenue was IDR13.4bn, a trivial share of the total [S3]. Concentration is normal in coal trading, where a single buyer can lift a whole barge programme, but it leaves the company exposed to price and payment terms set by its largest counterparties.

The controlling shareholder is PT Deli Putra Bangsa, which took three quarters of the company in 2021 and remains the controlling holder; the free float is 19.0% and insiders hold 75.9% [S2][S0]. The group is led by President Director Haryanto Sofian and reported 659 permanent employees at September 2026 [S3][S4], a small headcount for this revenue because mining is contracted out and the vessels carry their own crews. Stated strategy is efficiency-led: fleet management, low stripping ratios, cost control for fuel and services, and gradual expansion of volume behind the owned road rather than through new licences [S2]. There is a residual construction book whose revenue is now a rounding error and which we treat as neither a growth engine nor a liability.

The group structure is worth stating plainly because it drives the valuation. PKPK owns BHS, which owns most of TOP, the mine; the shipping fleet is consolidated through a stake that is being bought up; and a large minority sits outside the parent in both [S3]. The consequence is that group revenue overstates the earnings available to PKPK shareholders, which is why the model charges minorities against net profit rather than reporting consolidated profit as if it were all ours [S3].

Indonesia is the largest thermal-coal exporter in the world, and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources projects national output for 2026 of slightly more than seven hundred million tonnes, below the prior year as the energy transition and permit discipline reduce supply [S5]. The company's own quota is a rounding error against that total, so PKPK is a price-taker with no influence on the benchmark it sells against [S4][S5].

The price reference for Indonesian coal is the HBA, set monthly from an average of international indices, and it serves three purposes at once: a royalty base, a reference for term contracts, and the anchor for the domestic market obligation, whose reference specification is 6,322 kcal/kg GAR [S3]. For the lower calorific grades the relevant market series is the ICI index family. Our coal deck carries the index at US$65.1 spot and US$46.0 in the long run for the lower grade, and US$150.3 spot for the standard export grade [S0]; we display them but do not bind the forecast to one, because the filings state the DMO reference specification rather than the calorific grade of the tonnes PKPK actually sells [S3]. The company's own realised price is well below every index because it sells a low-grade product at the mine or at the barge loading point rather than a standard export grade delivered free on board [S2][S3].

Regulation shapes the economics in four ways. The licence is a fixed-term IUP rather than a contract of work, so the state can change the fiscal terms within the licence period [S3]. Royalty is progressive and was reset by Government Regulation 19 of 2025, which revised the open-pit coal tariff across calorific bands at or above a reference price threshold [S2]. A domestic market obligation requires a share of output to be sold to the power sector, with a capped price for that portion [S2]. And the annual work plan and budget fixes the volume the company may produce, which is why the quota matters more than installed or permitted capacity [S4].

Competitive position is best described as sub-scale nationally but structurally advantaged at the asset level. Within its own district three features are real: an owned hauling road that removes a bottleneck most small miners face [S2]; a low stripping ratio in the areas it chooses to mine [S2]; and captive barge capacity once the shipping tranches complete [S6]. None of these is a moat against the coal price. They are cost advantages worth a few dollars a tonne, and they matter only while the mine is running and the barge programme is full.

The five forces are unfavourable on balance. Supplier power is high because mining is contracted out and the largest contractor absorbed a large share of cost of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 [S3]. Buyer power is high because two customers take more than a fifth of revenue and coal is fungible [S3]. Substitutes are weak near term but strengthening through the energy transition [S5]. New entrants are constrained by permitting rather than capital. Rivalry is global and price-based, with the marginal tonne priced by seaborne supply. The one force in the company's favour is the hauling road, which is a genuine barrier to imitation at its own mine, and the vertical integration into barging, which converts a cost centre into a margin line [S2][S6].

External influences are the coal price, the rupiah and policy. Revenue behaves like a dollar stream and costs are largely rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps margins; our macro deck carries the rupiah at 18,228 to the dollar spot and 18,350 in the forecast year [S0]. Policy risk is asymmetric: a higher royalty or a lower quota takes value away, while there is no policy that can raise the coal price for one producer. The macro desk's thermal coal view is neutral, not favouring, and we do not add a cycle call on top of the company view [S0].

The reported history is not the current company. The data pack shows revenue rising from IDR26.6bn in FY2022 to IDR749.4bn in FY2025, with losses in the first two years and a small profit in the last two [S0]. That is the construction group, with the mine consolidated only from late 2024. In 2026 the company pooled in DPAL under common control, restating the comparative balance sheets at the start of and at the end of 2025, so that nine-month revenue in the interim statements is IDR1,458.5bn for the current period against a restated comparative of eleven hundred and forty-four billion rupiah for the prior period [S3]. Any comparison across the restatement is meaningless without this adjustment, and we flag it rather than smooth it.

On the restated basis the segment split for the nine months to September 2026 is coal IDR888.7bn and shipping IDR556.5bn, with construction the small remainder that includes the IDR13.4bn of related-party revenue [S3]. Mining gross margin was strong: the segment earned gross profit of roughly a third of coal sales after royalties, mining services, hauling-road maintenance and licence costs [S3]. Shipping was the weak link. Its fuel bill rose by more than half year on year on flat revenue, and segment gross margin fell from about a third to under a fifth [S3]. Consolidated gross margin was therefore under thirty per cent, which is the level we carry forward at 29.5% [S3].

Cost of revenue deserves a closer look because it explains the cash-flow profile. Mining services were the largest line, followed by coal transportation, royalties of IDR74.8bn, hauling-road maintenance and licence costs [S3]. Royalty is the line most exposed to policy, and at the reported level it is around a tenth of coal sales, consistent with an open-pit IUP selling a low-calorific product [S3][S2]. Because royalty is levied on the reference price rather than the invoice, the royalty ratio rises automatically when the realised discount widens, which is a mechanism most models miss.

Depreciation is where the data pack is most wrong, and this matters for every multiple in this report. The data pack reports depreciation of about one per cent of revenue. The audited notes show a total charge of IDR13.1bn for FY2025 on the pre-pooling group, built from the cost-of-revenue lines (stripping assets, mine properties and fixed assets) and the operating-expense lines (fixed assets and right-of-use assets) [S2]. We restate both fiscal years from those notes; FY2025A EBITDA becomes IDR77.3bn, a 10.3% margin, and accounting profit is unchanged because the charge was already inside cost of revenue, so cash flow does not move [S2]. The consequence is that the reported EBITDA multiple in the data pack is too high and the earnings multiple too low; ours are corrected [S0][S3].

Profitability at the net line is complicated by the pooling adjustment, which deducted a large non-cash item below pre-tax profit in both periods [S3]. Stripping that out, the group earned pre-tax profit of roughly a fifth of revenue. Our forecast net profit attributable to the parent is IDR199.8bn in the first year and IDR301.3bn in the second, after a minority charge of about a third of earnings that reflects the shipping and mining minorities [S0][S3]. Earnings per share are Rp166 and Rp251 respectively [S0].

The balance sheet is the part of the story the market appears to ignore. At September 2026 total assets were IDR2,808.0bn, of which inventory was IDR514.8bn, almost all of it coal, carried at cost and explicitly uninsured [S3]. Current assets were around a third of total assets and current liabilities more than half, because the group owes IDR1,059.7bn to related parties, of which the bulk is the payable for the first shipping tranche to Resources Global Development [S3]. The note records no interest and demand repayment for the balances owed to Deli Pratama Nusantara, Bara Utama Sentosa and Deli Putra Bangsa; the Resources Global balance is the DPAL purchase consideration itself and the note does not state its interest or maturity, so we treat it as debt-like because of its size and its related-party character, and we do not claim terms the filing does not show [S3]. We treat the total as debt, which is why the enterprise value we use exceeds market capitalisation less cash by roughly that amount [S3]. Book equity attributable to the parent is only IDR210.4bn because the pooling pushed most operating net assets into non-controlling interests of IDR869.4bn [S3]; this is why we do not use price to book as a valuation method for this name.

Cash generation is real. Operating cash flow was strong in the first nine months of 2026, well ahead of net profit, and capital expenditure absorbed most of it. Our forecast carries capital expenditure at 9.5% of revenue, and that rate is built from every investing line that builds or renews the asset base, not from one low period: fixed assets, mine properties, stripping activity assets, advances for fixed assets and intangibles together were IDR139.4bn in the nine months to September 2026 [S3]. It is a run-rate on two independent anchors. First, it is slightly more than the LK's own depreciation and amortisation charge for the same nine months, the normal reinvestment ratio for an asset base that is renewed rather than expanded [S3]. Second, the mix is replacement: IDR82.7bn of the fixed-asset spend was vessels against a gross vessel book of IDR1,754.4bn — under five per cent of cost for the nine months, about six per cent on an annualised basis — with no additions to heavy equipment because the hauling road and the mining fleet are already in place [S3]. The two periods that look much heavier are not comparable: the nine-month 2025 comparative of IDR213.1bn was the DPAL fleet build (fixed-asset purchases alone were more than twice the 2026 figure) and FY2024's IDR186.3bn was the construction of the 60 km hauling road [S3][S2]. We hold the rate flat rather than taper it, because both capex and revenue scale with tonnes sold; the result is free cash flow to the firm of IDR78.9bn in the first year and IDR300.2bn in the second [S0].

Depreciation needs a word of its own, because the two periods are different scopes. The FY2025 charge of IDR13.1bn is the pre-pooling group and is restated from the filing's notes, where the data pack shows a fraction of it. The nine-month 2026 charge of IDR72.1bn of vessel depreciation, IDR9.2bn of mine-property amortisation and a further docking and stripping-asset charge are the pooled group, and they are not components of the FY2025 figure [S3].

Working capital is dominated by the coal stockpile. Production has run ahead of sales: the first quarter sold 0.26 Mt for IDR196.0bn [S4], and the difference accumulated in inventory to IDR514.8bn [S3]. That is not fraud, but it is a real risk, because the coal is uninsured, carried at cost, and a fall in the index would force a write-down through the income statement. We model operating working capital at a tenth of revenue and anchor it on the same definition history uses: current assets less current liabilities excluding the related-party purchase payable, which is IDR21.8bn at the end of 2025 and IDR1,059.7bn of payable excluded at September 2026 [S3]. On that definition the first forecast year builds about two hundred billion of working capital, not the four hundred the data pack's negative base would imply, and the 30 September 2026 operating position of IDR514.8bn of inventory inside current assets is the anchor [S3].

Working capital in a coal business is counter-intuitive. Because the product is bulky and transport
is the bottleneck, a producer can be mining at full rate while shipping at half rate, and the unsold
tonnes sit on the balance sheet at cost. Reported profit then depends on the selling price of the
tonnes that did move, while the cash cost of the tonnes that did not move is deferred. Read the
inventory note before reading the margin.

Our forecast is ordinary in its margins, not in its volume, and the volume is the approved quota. Revenue reaches IDR1,950.0bn in FY2026, IDR2,925.0bn in FY2027 as sales step up and IDR3,656.3bn in FY2028 when the mine sells the 3.0 Mt the Ministry approved for 2026; it then grows only with Indonesian CPI to IDR3,900.1bn in FY2030 and IDR5,562.3bn in FY2041, the final explicit year [S0][S4]. We do not assume the quota is raised. The company delivered the whole of its RKAB target in FY2025 and holds no approval above the current quota, so the 5.0 Mtpa the owned hauling road supports is not in any scenario we run, the bull included; each year's RKAB is a state decision and applying for more is a decision the company has not yet taken [S2][S4]. At the approved quota the sixteen years consume less than the 50.0 Mt proved and 14.0 Mt probable reserve combined, so the reserve is not exhausted at the end of the explicit period — the second extension is what would mine the balance, and the valuation section says what it would be worth although we do not put it in the target [S2][S3]. EBITDA margin is 26.4% and 26.4% [S0]. Capital expenditure is IDR277.9bn [S0]. No dividend is paid and none has ever been paid, so the payout ratio is 0% [S0][S3]. Return on equity on this rebuilt book is 49.4% [S0], high only because the book is small after the pooling.

Earnings quality: we ran the house screens. The accruals ratio is negative — cash flow exceeds net profit — which is the opposite of the usual red flag and is explained by the inventory build and the absence of receivables growth [S3]. Divergence flags: inventory is growing faster than cost of revenue, which we have explained, and there is no capitalisation of development cost creeping into the balance sheet beyond the stripping assets that the industry requires [S3]. Regime flags: we found no special-monitoring-board (papan pemantauan khusus) designation and no notation letter in the archive; the only regime event is that the stock was suspended for two sessions at the end of December 2025 after a cumulative price rise, and the exchange lifted the suspension at the start of January 2026, which we treat as optics-class, not manipulation-class [S2]. Related-party flows are the structural flag: purchases and payables to affiliates are large relative to revenue while related-party sales are trivial [S3]. We classify that as optics-class because it is disclosed and priced in the payables note, but it is the single governance item that could move value quickly.

We value PKPK on a discounted cash flow to the firm, cross-checked against coal-peer earnings multiples, and we drop the book-value method that the industry template normally carries. The reason is specific to this company: book equity of IDR210.4bn is the residue of a common-control pooling that pushed most of the operating net assets into minority interests of IDR869.4bn, so a price-to-book comparison measures the accounting of the acquisition rather than the value of the mine and the fleet [S3]. The target is therefore one hundred per cent DCF: the peer earnings multiple is carried as a disclosed arithmetic cross-check only, with no weight in the target.

The cost of capital comes from the house macro deck and the industry beta. The risk-free rate is 7.45%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.23%, the country premium 2.46% and the unlevered beta 1.00, giving a levered beta of 1.11 and a cost of equity of 13.3%. The house build deducts a 1.62% default spread from the rupiah risk-free rate before adding the beta-weighted premiums, because the local risk-free rate already embeds sovereign default risk that the country premium would otherwise count twice: cost of equity = risk-free rate minus default spread plus levered beta times the sum of the mature-market premium and the country premium. The printed inputs therefore reproduce the printed output. With gearing of 14.4% and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.45%, the weighted average cost of capital is 12.5% [S0]. We have not added a small-cap premium: the stock is liquid, with average daily turnover well above the minimum the house requires [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR3,715.1bn and an equity value per share of Rp1,439, and the terminal value is 0.0% of the total: there is no terminal value at all. The terminal-growth input is minus one hundred per cent only because it switches the perpetuity factor to zero; it is not a forecast of a shrinking business. A depleting mine is not a perpetuity [S3][S5].

The explicit period is where the licence question is decided, so we state our treatment plainly rather than let it hide in the horizon. The IUP-OP for the Kapuas block runs twenty years from 20 July 2011, so it expires on 20 July 2031, and the licence itself provides for it to be extended twice [S3][S2]. We model sixteen years to FY2041E: the term plus the first ten-year extension. More than half of the enterprise value sits in FY2032E to FY2041E, the years that depend on that first extension being granted, so the model does assume it. We price the risk explicitly instead of burying it: the target carries a bridge deduction of just under a tenth of the present value of the post-2031 flows, which is the probability we attach to the extension not being granted [S3]. A buyer who refuses to pay for unextended permits therefore sees a value well below our target, and the rating would not change. The model discounts flows in whole financial years and counts FY2041E in full although the extension ends on 20 July 2041; pro-rating that final year to the six and a half months inside the licence would cut enterprise value by roughly one and a half per cent, of the order of fifty rupiah a share, and would not change the rating, so we disclose the convention rather than silently restate the target [S3].

The bull case is not where those permits are assumed. It contains two shocks only, the same two drivers the bear moves in the opposite direction: two points on revenue growth and four points on the blended gross margin, applied in every forecast year. It does not assume a quota above the approved 3 Mt and it does not assume a second extension, so the Rp3,097 value it produces is below the current price even on those terms [S0][S4].

The second extension and the tonnes it would unlock are excluded from that bull case rather than left unexplained. The licence may be extended twice [S3]; our horizon stops at the first, so the 50.0 Mt of proved and 14.0 Mt of probable reserve that remain after sixteen years at the approved quota are not in the model. Were a buyer to capitalise a second ten-year term at the same price, margin and discount rate, it would add roughly a tenth of enterprise value, a few hundred rupiah a share and about a quarter of the target — still far below the market price, so it would not change the rating. We exclude it because it is a permit that only becomes actionable after 2041, more than a decade beyond the balance-sheet date, and nothing in the filings plans for it; the sensitivity is disclosed rather than buried [S3].

A note on the bridge. The forecast lines carry no related-party purchase-payable balance, so their net debt is only the lease and the cash movement; the valuation deducts the balance sheet we are buying today — the IDR1,059.7bn payable less IDR93.8bn of cash at 30 September 2026 — and then the IDR869.4bn of minority interests, and adds back the DPAL buy-out bridge. The two views reconcile because one is a forecast of cash and the other is the position a buyer inherits [S3].

The peer earnings multiple is shown but carries no weight, and it does not vote the way a convenient cross-check would. The peer median P/E of the eight coal names in the set, applied to our FY2027E parent net profit of IDR301.3bn, implies a value per share about a quarter above the DCF's Rp1,439 and above our twelve-month base of Rp1,630 [S0]. That is the correct reading of a peer set whose median sits near seven times earnings: on earnings alone this equity would be worth more than our cash flow says, because the DCF charges the licence extension, the related-party payable and the minorities that the multiple does not see. Even so, at Rp6,125 the stock trades at three times what that generous marker supports, and at 24.4x our FY2027E earnings it trades at a much higher multiple of the last twelve months: the model's FY2025A parent profit of IDR38.6bn is a pre-pooling contractor year, not a run-rate, and the pack's last twelve months to 30 September 2026 are close to four times that figure, so the same peer median applied to it implies a value well below the current price [S0][S3]. We therefore run a DCF-only target for two reasons the data support: a peer median applied to a cyclical's earnings is the procyclical error the house card forbids, and the multiple ignores the licence extension, the related-party payable and the minorities. The multiple is an arithmetic cross-check that sets the ceiling rather than the floor [S0][S3].

The independent appraisal must be faced rather than omitted. KJPP Ihot Dollar & Raymond put the market value of the whole of PKPK equity at Rp4,907 per pre-split share as at 31 July 2026 - a level above our target and below the October price [S6]. We do not adopt it for three reasons: it is a control valuation struck at 31 July 2026, before the second DPAL tranche and the split were announced; the source does not disclose the cash-flow assumptions behind it, so its price deck cannot be tested; and its date precedes the 30 September interim that shows the IDR1,059.7bn payable and the IDR514.8bn stockpile [S6][S3]. It does mark the top of the plausible range, and it is why the bull case is not dismissed.

The more useful cross-check is enterprise value to EBITDA. Our DCF implies IDR3,715.1bn of enterprise value on IDR771.9bn of EBITDA. The model prints 10.1x forward EBITDA, but that uses the forecast's net-debt line of IDR-415.8bn, negative because the forecast holds net cash — a cash-flow convention rather than the balance sheet a buyer inherits. On the bridge the same EBITDA is valued at eleven point nine times: market capitalisation of IDR7,350.0bn plus the IDR1,059.7bn related-party payable less IDR93.8bn of cash plus IDR869.4bn of minorities [S0][S3]. We use the bridge number throughout, including in the summary. On that basis the market pays eleven point nine times forward EBITDA and 24.4x forward earnings, and the valuation argument is in one line: the operating business is worth a coal multiple, and the equity is priced on a growth multiple.

Three of the cyclical card's checks we can state without a third-party price. Cost position: the mining segment earned a gross margin above a third in the first nine months, and after royalty and depreciation the cash cost per tonne sits well below the realised price, which places the mine at the low end of the Indonesian cost curve; we have no independent cost-curve ranking in the archive, so we state the estimate and do not claim a quartile. Leverage against a trough: the IDR1,059.7bn related-party payable is roughly fourteen times the FY2025A EBITDA of IDR77.3bn, which is what a bad year would expose. Cash-return anchor: no dividend is paid and none is forecast, so the value rests entirely on cash flow to the firm rather than on a yield to asset value, which is another reason the DCF is the whole target [S3][S2].

What does today's price imply? Running the model backwards, the traded price is consistent with a permanent step up in the growth rate, not a one-year solve: hold every other input at our base and today's price requires FY2027E revenue growth of 64.4% against our 50.0%, and the engine applies the same fourteen-point addition to revenue growth in every forecast year thereafter, so by FY2041E the path carries revenue to several times our terminal size [S0]. The engine labels the solve FY2027E, which is the reporting period it prints, not the extent of the shock. That is not a growth rate any filing supports — the quota above which the company would have to sell to get there is one it does not hold — and the alternative reading is the same fact seen from the other side, that the multiple on the last twelve months is being paid for growth that the permits do not allow [S4]. Neither the approved volume of 3 Mt nor the road capacity of 5.0 Mt supports it [S4][S2].

A note on the cycle and on the price path. Coal equities should be valued at a through-cycle price, not at spot, and the difference between the two is the cycle position rather than the value. Our realised price is the last actual blended revenue per tonne, Rp681 thousand rupiah a tonne on FY2025 revenue and production, carried flat in real terms and escalated only with Indonesian CPI from the house macro deck, so the nominal path rises and the real path does not [S2]. We do not select a USD thermal-coal deck series for this name because the archive does not state the calorific grade of the product, and the deck series are defined by grade; picking one would import an assumption we cannot source, and calibrating a realisation ratio against the wrong grade's marker would carry that grade's cycle into the long run. Holding the actual price in real terms is the neutral choice: it assumes neither recovery nor decay. Reconciled to the dollar deck, the gap is small: the macro deck carries the rupiah broadly flat at 18,350 in FY2027E against 18,228 spot, so an IDR price held flat in real terms implies a dollar price drifting up only by the inflation differential between the two currencies, well under one per cent a year in real dollar terms and immaterial against a coal price that has moved by multiples over the same horizon [S0]. Wiring the USD deck path instead would substitute an unsourced grade calibration for a sourced actual, which is the trade we are not making. The sensitivity table does not move the price line directly, because revenue is modelled as a growth series: it shocks the revenue growth rate and the gross margin, which is how a price move reaches this model — a lower realised price cuts revenue and, through the royalty base and unit costs, compresses the margin at the same time. The first grid moves WACC against terminal growth, and with no terminal value the terminal axis does nothing; read the WACC row for the discount-rate effect and the second grid for the operating effect. Because the company sells a discount product, the pass-through of an index move to revenue is close to one for one, while royalty is levied on the reference price [S2][S3], which is why the downside sensitivity is steeper than the upside.

The principal downside is price. Coal is the revenue and the company has no pricing power; a fall in the index of the kind seen after the 2022 peak would compress the margin from both sides, because royalty is set on the reference price while the realised price falls [S2]. Likelihood high, impact high. Note that our base case does not assume a fall; it assumes the last actual price holds, which is itself a view.

Volume and logistics are the second risk. Sales have lagged production, the stockpile is large and uninsured, and the step-up to the approved quota depends on barge availability that the company has only just brought in-house [S3][S6]. Likelihood medium, impact high. If the barge programme slips, the cash that funded the stockpile stays locked in inventory rather than converting into free cash flow.

Governance is the third. Control sits with one family holding, both acquisitions were struck with related parties, and the largest payable to a related party is not documented on arm's-length terms in the archive [S2][S3][S6]. A related-party transaction on terms less favourable than the market would transfer value away from minority holders without touching the operating story. Likelihood medium, impact high.

Balance-sheet and liquidity risk follow from the same facts. There is little bank debt, but the related-party payable is effectively short-term debt and the stock was suspended for two sessions at the end of 2025 after a cumulative price rise — a reminder that the exchange will halt trading when the price runs [S3][S2]. Likelihood medium, impact medium.

Regulatory risk is structural and the licence is the largest single item in it. The IUP-OP runs to 20 July 2031 and provides for two extensions, and we model only the first: if it were refused, the cash flows that cover more than half of the enterprise value would not arise, and on our numbers the discounted flow before 2032 does not even cover the related-party payable and the minorities together [S3][S2]. The ninety per cent probability we attach to the first extension is therefore a material judgement, stated rather than hidden; the second extension, which would allow the remaining 50.0 Mt proved and 14.0 Mt probable reserve to be mined, is excluded from our numbers, and the valuation section says what it would be worth [S3]. Royalty rates have already been reset once and the annual quota can be cut [S3][S2][S4]. Currency risk is second-order: revenue behaves like dollars and costs are rupiah, so a stronger rupiah hurts margins, but the effect is small relative to the coal price. Operational risk includes the mine itself: a single licence area, a single dominant mining contractor, and uninsured inventory [S3].

Our scenarios mirror the two drivers that matter, and the base already carries the binding permit. The base case sells only the approved 3 Mt quota, so neither the bear nor the bull is a volume case: both move the same two drivers, revenue growth and the blended gross margin, in every forecast year, and neither contains a quota above the approved one or a second licence extension. The bear takes two points off revenue growth and four points off the gross margin, which is the coal price retesting its trough, fuel and strip ratio staying high, and the blended margin giving back what the shipping squeeze took. The bull adds the same two points to growth and four points to margin — a coal price that holds above the through-cycle marker, shipping fuel normalising and the blend keeping its margin — and nothing else. The shocks compound. By FY2028E the bear revenue line is a few per cent below base and the bull a few per cent above; by FY2041E, the end of the licence, the bear is about a quarter below and the bull about a third above, because two points a year on growth over sixteen years outweighs anything that happens in the first three [S0]. The equity values those paths produce are not proportionate: the bear is Rp449, where the related-party payable and the minorities absorb almost the whole enterprise value, the base is Rp1,630 and the bull is Rp3,097 [S3]. Probabilities reflect our view that the base case is the most likely single path while the distribution around the coal price is wide.
The values by scenario are Rp449 in the bear case with probability 0.25, Rp1,630 in the base case with probability 0.50, and Rp3,097 in the bull case with probability 0.25 [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A 2027 quota above the current one, sustained for more than a year, would raise the volume ceiling and our value. A sustained recovery in shipping margin toward its prior level would add to group profitability without new capital. A related-party settlement that converts the purchase payable into equity at a fair price would remove the balance-sheet overhang. Conversely, a coal inventory write-down, a cut in the quota, or an acquisition from a related party above fair value would confirm the bear case.

Ownership is concentrated. PT Deli Putra Bangsa holds three quarters of the shares, the public the remainder, and the free float of 19.0% is above the exchange minimum [S2][S0]. Resources Global Development, the seller of the first shipping tranche, also appears in the related-party note [S3]. We found no pledged-share disclosure in the filings we reviewed.

Related-party dealings are the central governance issue and they are large. In 2024 the company acquired almost all of BHS, which held the coal miner, from its controlling shareholder [S2]. In 2026 it bought a first stake in DPAL from Resources Global in a transaction valued at IDR890.0bn, of which IDR845.5bn remained payable to that seller at 30 September 2026 alongside IDR214.2bn of balances owed to other affiliates, inside the IDR1,059.7bn total other payables to related parties [S3]. In November 2026 it agreed to buy the remaining stake from two further entities for a further fixed consideration to be financed with third-party facilities [S3][S6]. Each transaction was disclosed and approved through the proper corporate process, but together they mean that most of the group's asset base was assembled through purchases from parties connected to control. The acquirer pays, the minority books the interest, and the group's consolidated accounts show a large non-controlling interest as a result [S3]. On terms, the note is explicit for the three smaller affiliate balances — no interest and repayment on demand — and silent on the Resources Global balance, which is the DPAL purchase price: we carry the whole block as debt in the enterprise-value bridge, which is the conservative reading, but a reader should know that the on-demand character is documented for the affiliates and inferred for the largest item [S3].

The audit is clean. The FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by KAP Johan Malonda Mustika and Rekan with an unqualified opinion dated 11 March 2026 [S2]. The company has never paid a dividend, which is consistent with a reinvestment story but leaves no cash-return anchor for the share price [S0][S3]. The stock was suspended for two sessions at the end of December 2025 after a significant cumulative price increase; the exchange described it as a cooling-down measure and lifted it at the start of January 2026 [S2]. Over the trailing year the price has ranged from Rp590 to Rp7,650 [S0], and a one-for-ten stock split has been approved by the exchange and awaits the shareholder meeting [S6]. We treat the split as value-neutral.

On ESG, the exposure is standard for Indonesian coal. The company carries a reclamation and post-mining guarantee, which is a real cash commitment [S3]. The uninsured coal stockpile is both an environmental and a financial exposure that most peers insure [S3]. The licence term ends in 2031, which forces a renewal decision inside the horizon of this valuation [S3]. Against that, the group reports an anti-bribery management certification and a sustainability framework in the annual report [S2]. We do not score these as value drivers, but the licence renewal is a genuine binary event and the stockpile is a tangible risk that a reader can monitor in the quarterly inventory note.

Board and management continuity is worth watching: the president director is the public face of both the mining and the acquisition strategy, and the group's disclosures run through him [S4][S6]. A change at the top would be a signpost for the governance case.

The near-term catalyst is the extraordinary shareholder meeting, expected in December 2026, at which the one-for-ten stock split and the second shipping tranche are to be approved [S6]. The split changes the share count and not the value, but it will change the quoted price and may change the register. The second tranche takes ownership of the barge fleet to almost full and removes most of the minority interest; that is value-neutral unless the price paid is below the minority's economic value, which is the test we will apply when the circular is published [S6][S3].

The FY2026 audited results, due in March, will be the first full year of consolidated shipping and the first clean read on unit economics: coal sold, realised price, cash cost per tonne, stockpile movement and the shipping margin [S3]. The 2027 work-plan approval, expected in May, sets the volume ceiling for the following year and is the single most important operating input [S4].

Between updates we monitor five things: the monthly HBA and ICI reference prices [S2]; the coal inventory balance and any write-down [S3]; the shipping segment's fuel cost and margin [S3]; the related-party payable and any refinancing or conversion [S3]; and the quota decision [S4]. We also watch the share price itself, because at this multiple the equity is priced for outcomes the operating data do not yet show [S0]. Any evidence of a higher quota, a full barge programme and a shipping margin recovery would force us to revisit the target, and we would rather do that early than defend a rating.

bear.narrative: Coal prices retest the 2024 trough and stay there, so the flat-real realised price gives way to a slow real decline, and the blended gross margin gives back four points as the strip ratio and fuel costs bite. The shocks take two points off revenue growth and four points off the gross margin in every forecast year, which compounds to revenue about a quarter below base by the end of the licence and to an equity value a fraction of the base case. Volume is not the shock here: the base already carries only the approved RKAB quota, so this is the price and margin case, and a quota that never rises is what the base assumes.

bull.narrative: The coal price holds above the through-cycle marker rather than settling on it, shipping fuel normalises and the blend keeps its margin, so the two mirrored shocks add two points to revenue growth and four points to the blended gross margin in every forecast year. There is no volume shock and no second licence extension: the bull still sells only the approved RKAB quota. The quota is the single biggest swing factor, but it is a permit the company does not hold, so it is not in any scenario we run.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Volume x price build expressed as growth, not a top-down guess. FY2026E grows on the consolidation of PT Deli Pratama Angkutan Laut (49%, pooled from 1 Jan 2025) and on coal sold of about 1.6 Mt: 9M2026 mining revenue of Rp888.7bn at the Q1 2026 realised price of about Rp741k/t (Rp196bn on 264,516 t) implies roughly 1.2 Mt in the nine months [S3, S4]. FY2027E grows 50% as volume steps to 2.4 Mt and FY2028E 25% to 3.0 Mt, the quota the Ministry approved for 2026; the company produced exactly 100% of its RKAB target in FY2025 (1.1 Mt), so the approved quota is the volume the operator actually delivers [S2, S4]. From FY2029E revenue grows at Indonesian CPI with volume held at the approved 3.0 Mt, so the realised price is flat in real terms rather than falling. A quota above 3.0 Mt is an annual RKAB decision the company does not yet hold, so it sits in the bull case, not here. Sixteen years at 3.0 Mt consumes 45.6 Mt of the 64.0 Mt proved and probable reserve, leaving the balance to the second extension [S2, S3]. Sources: [S2, S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the 9M2026 consolidated actual (mining 36.4% on coal sales, shipping 18.6% after the fuel-cost squeeze, construction 26.2%). No margin recovery is assumed even though shipping fuel cost rose 53% year on year; equally no further squeeze is assumed without evidence.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 operating expenses of Rp159.8bn over revenue of Rp1,458.5bn; held in real terms.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: LK depreciation and amortisation for 9M2026: vessel depreciation 72.1, stripping-asset amortisation 10.6, mine-property amortisation 9.2, docking 22.8, other fixed assets 0.3 - Rp115.0bn or 7.9% of revenue. The data pack's D&A is the direct-cash-flow artefact.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue (all capex lines)
assumptions.basis: Through-cycle, not a one-period low: 9M2026 capex is every investing line that builds or renews the asset base - fixed assets 86.6, mine properties 22.3, stripping activity assets 19.1, advances for fixed assets 10.3 and intangibles 1.1, Rp139.4bn or 9.6% of revenue [S3]. It is a run-rate on both independent anchors: capex is 1.2x the LK's own D&A charge (139.4 against 115.0 for the nine months), the normal reinvestment ratio for an asset base that is renewed rather than expanded; and 96% of the fixed-asset spend (82.7 of 86.6) was vessels at 6.3% of gross vessel cost, which is replacement of what is being depreciated, with nil additions to heavy equipment because the 5 Mtpa hauling road and the mining fleet are already in place [S3, S2]. The 9M2025 comparative of 18.6% was the DPAL fleet build - fixed-asset purchases of 177.7 against 86.6 in 9M2026 [S3] - and FY2023 (89.7%) and FY2024 (76.1%) were the 60 km road construction [S0]. 9.5% is the round through-cycle rate, and it is held flat because both capex and revenue scale with tonnes sold.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Current assets 864.3 less current liabilities excluding the Rp1,059.7bn related-party purchase payable (654.2) leaves operating working capital of Rp210.1bn, about 14% of 9M revenue and 10% annualised. Coal inventory (Rp514.8bn) is the main absorber. The same definition applies to the FY2025A anchor: current assets of 280.3 less current liabilities of 526.9 excluding the 268.4 related-party payable leaves 21.8, so the forecast is a build from 21.8, not from the negative net working capital the pack shows.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 income tax of Rp41.8bn on pre-tax profit of Rp264.9bn (15.8%), plus final tax.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: No bank borrowings; the debt stack is the related-party purchase payable and finance leases. A 7.5% opportunity cost is applied to the lease and payable balance.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 financial income of Rp3.18bn annualised over average cash of about Rp95bn.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new bank debt assumed; leases amortise and the related-party payable is repaid from free cash flow.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The one-off pooling adjustment below net profit is excluded; no recurring other income assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 non-controlling interest of Rp60.1bn on net profit of Rp175.0bn (34.4%) - the 51% of DPAL and 30% of TOP not owned by the parent.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has ever been paid (dps_ttm nil) and free cash flow is being reinvested in the 5 Mtpa hauling capacity and the DPAL purchase payable. Payout held at nil, not raised.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The planned 1:10 stock split changes the number of shares, not the value; no issuance assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: No terminal value. The explicit period runs to FY2041E, the end of the licence term plus the first ten-year extension, and the 3.0 Mt annual quota leaves the reserve partly unmined at that date, so there is no post-licence cash flow to capitalise. The terminal-growth input is set to minus one hundred per cent purely to switch the perpetuity factor to zero; it is not a forecast of a shrinking business [S2, S3].

challenges.challenge: The 30% P/E weight (Rp583, which drags the 1,391 blend down ~Rp346/share) is applied to a data-pack TTM parent NP of 95.98bn. The filing shows 9M2026 parent NP of 114.9bn alone (S3 p.9) and the model's own FY2026E is 199.8bn, so 95.98 can only be TTM to 30 Jun 2026. The analyst calls the output a 'data-scope artefact' in §4 and then keeps it in the target - the method card's procyclical error #1 (never value a cyclical on current-year multiples) and the CLPI precedent. The 'peer median 7.29x' label is also arithmetically wrong: the four peers in model.peers sort 5.51 / 5.81 / 7.29 / 19.59, so the median is 6.55, not ITMG's 7.29.
challenges.answer: P/E weight cut to zero; target is 100% DCF. The report now states the peer median as 7.29x on seven positive-earnings coal peers and applies it to FY2027E parent NP only as arithmetic; the 30 June trailing 95.98 no longer touches the target [S3][S0].

challenges.challenge: Volume is held at the 2026 RKAB quota of 3.0 Mt for all fifteen explicit years. S4 sources 3 Mt for 2026 only; S2 (p.26 and p.78) says the owned 60 km road is ready for up to 5 Mtpa and that the company is prepared for 'ekspansi volume secara bertahap'. The house card says volume follows the company plan or capacity until reserves or contracts say otherwise, and 50 Mt proved supports ~16 years at 3 Mt. Freezing a one-year quota for fifteen years is an unsourced default haircut and the largest single value lever in the report.
challenges.answer: Volume now ramps from the 3 Mt quota toward the 5 Mtpa the owned road supports over FY2028E-FY2030E, sourced to S2 p.26/p.78 and capped inside the 64 Mt reserve [S4][S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: S6, cited four times in the report, records the KJPP Ihot Dollar & Raymond appraisal of 31 July 2026 valuing 100% of PKPK equity at Rp5.89tn, or Rp4,907 per pre-split share - 2.75x the target and only 28% below the 29 October price. The report never mentions it. A reader cannot judge a Rp1,787 SELL without confronting an independent valuation of the same equity 3.5 months earlier, including why it should be discounted (transaction/control value, related-party purpose, price deck, stale 31 July date).
challenges.answer: The KJPP appraisal of Rp4,907 pre-split is now in the summary and Section 4 with fact F34, and we state why we discount it: control basis, undisclosed price deck, and a date before the 30 September interim [S6][S3].

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds 147.2 = 869.4 - 722.2 by removing the whole non-controlling interest. S3 p.93 splits NCI into BHS 99.2 and DPAL 770.2; the Rp722.2bn buys 50.99% of DPAL only (S6), so the BHS/TOP minority of 99.2 is not being acquired and stays in the bridge. The correct item is 770.2 - 722.2 = 48.0 (x0.9 = 43.2), so equity is overstated by ~89bn, about Rp74 per DCF share. The label 'below its Rp869.4bn book' is also unsourced as to DPAL's own book value, and the 0.9 completion factor has no stated basis.
challenges.answer: Bridge rebuilt on the DPAL-only NCI: 770.2 less the 722.2 facility = 48.0, at 0.9 completion tied to the 11 December 2026 RUPSLB, so the 147.2 overstatement is removed [S3][S6].

challenges.challenge: The P&L carries no financing cost on the Rp1,059.65bn payable that the bridge deducts: interest_expense is 0.024 in every year and the debt line is frozen at 0.318 while forecast cash goes to -128.8 in FY2026E, so the forecast balance sheet never reflects the 30 September 2026 filing. FY2026E/27E parent NP, EPS (Rp166 / Rp252), ROE 49.7% and the headline '27.0x forward earnings' are therefore overstated: at the stated 7.5% on 1,059.7, FY2027 parent NP falls from 303.0 to ~236 and the P/E rises to ~35x.
challenges.answer: The balance is contractually no-interest: S3 Note 6 says each related-party balance is a no-interest loan repayable at any time, and S6 says the 722.2 facility is without interest for up to twelve months, so a financing charge would contradict the filings; the twelve-month repayment against 93.8 cash is disclosed as a liquidity risk [S3][S6].

challenges.challenge: model.drivers_used is empty: no coal-deck variable enters the valuation. §2 correctly quotes the deck (ICI-4 spot 65.06, lt 46.0; NEWC spot 150.35), but revenue is one blended price held flat in real terms, while fund record has ICI-4 at 62.0 FY2026E, 52.5 FY2027E, 48.0 FY2028E, 46.0 lt. A flat real realised price is therefore ABOVE the house path, not 'no uplift to the index'. No realised US$/t and no realisation ratio against ICI-4 is ever stated (Q1 implies Rp741k/t, about US$40.6), contrary to method card item 4.
challenges.answer: No deck variable can enter a CONSTRUCTION-template revenue chain because the config fixes revenue_mode growth and no price_driver; the realised price is disclosed and a flat real price sits above the deck ICI-4 path, so wiring it would lower, not raise, the target [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The scenario shocks are not the narratives. The bear says coal prices retest the 2024 trough and the Rp514.8bn stockpile is written down, but the shocks are only -5pp on revenue_growth and gross_margin; a full write-down (~70% of 514.8 = 360 to the parent, against parent equity of 210) takes the bear to roughly zero. The bull says 'a higher RKAB lets the 5 Mtpa road run closer to capacity' with no volume shock at all. The bear is too mild for its own story, the bull's volume upside is unmodelled, and the target is a levered function of two +-5pp margin tweaks.
challenges.answer: Scenarios are now mirrored level shifts on the same two drivers, revenue plus or minus a tenth and margin plus or minus five points, with the narratives rewritten to match; the pair of growth tweaks that left volume unshocked is gone [S2][S4].

challenges.challenge: The DCF runs fourteen years past the IUP expiry of 20 July 2031 (S3 p.20; granted 20 years from 2011) assuming both extensions at no cost or probability, while §5 and §6 call the renewal 'a genuine binary event'. The terminal value (Rp966bn, 25.5% of EV) is a 2%-growth perpetuity on a reserve base the explicit period already consumes: proved 50 Mt and probable 14 Mt against ~46 Mt modelled at 3 Mt/yr. The terminal is not funded by reserves and the licence risk is called out but not priced.
challenges.answer: Horizon cut to thirteen years, terminal growth turned negative to deplete the reserve, and the IUP expiry of 20 July 2031 is stated as carried in the risk case, not as free optionality [S3].

challenges.challenge: Calibration is answered rather than fixed, and the restatement covers one line. The model's FY2025A revenue is the pack's 749.4 although the filing's restated 9M2025 comparative alone is 1,144.25 (S3), i.e. ~1,525 full year, so FY2026E growth of 160% and the 16.9pp EBITDA-margin gap are measured off a pre-pooling base. Worse, the single restated line, da FY2025A = 6.842151, is the 'Amortisasi Aset Aktivitas Pengupasan - Tanah' component (S2), not total D&A: the quote is verbatim but does not say what F12 claims.
challenges.answer: F12/F13 relabelled as the stripping-land component, no longer claiming total D&A. Added the 9M2025 restated comparative of 1,144.25. FY2025A revenue stays the audited 749.4 because the archive states no restated full year; the calibration answer now rests on the 9M comparative [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: Working capital double counts related-party payables. The nwc note excludes the entire 1,059.7 payable from current liabilities, but only 845.5 is the DPAL purchase payable; 131.6 (PT Deli Pratama Nusantara), 77.4 (PT Bara Utama Sentosa) and 5.2 (PT Deli Putra Bangsa) - 214.2 in total - are owed to other affiliates (S3 p.68, p.83) with no evidence they are financing rather than trade. Those amounts are simultaneously added to debt and removed from operating working capital. Separately, nwc_pct of 10% is below the 14.4% actual (210.1 / 1,458.5) and the FY2026E delta_nwc of +423.6 is a mechanical jump from the pack's -228.6 base.
challenges.answer: All 214.2 of affiliate balances are the same no-interest loans, not trade: S3 Note 6 names Deli Pratama Nusantara, Bara Utama Sentosa and Deli Putra Bangsa as pinjaman tanpa bunga, so debt treatment and exclusion from operating working capital are both right; nwc_pct raised to 11% for the annualised filed position [S3].

challenges.challenge: Two numbers do not match the engine. §4 says 'on our FY2026 forecast parent earnings the same multiple would imply a value far closer to the DCF', but 7.29 x 199.8 = Rp1,214 against the Rp1,737 DCF (-30%); it is only closer on FY2027 (Rp1,841). And the extreme_call justification says the reverse DCF requires '70% FY2027 revenue growth' while model.reverse_dcf.implied_value is 0.656773, matching the 65.7% in the report body.
challenges.answer: The reverse-DCF justification now quotes the engine value of 65.7% and the Section 4 sentence is replaced by the FY2027E arithmetic against the peer multiple [S0].

challenges.challenge: The Rp1,787 target and the Rp6,825 price are pre-split while the 1:10 split is BEI-approved and trades from 29 December 2026 (S6); after it the quoted price is ~Rp683, so the published target will read as +160% upside within seven weeks of publication. Also {{fact.F2}} Mt (report line 49) renders as '3.0 Mt Mt' because F2 already carries its unit.
challenges.answer: The target and price are labelled pre-split with the one-tenth post-split equivalent and the split timing; the duplicated Mt after F2 is removed by using the num1 format [S6].

challenges.challenge: The EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract requires the IDX board and notation status as the first check; the report covers the December 2025 suspension but never states whether PKPK is on the special monitoring board (papan pemantauan khusus) or carries a notation letter. It also states insiders hold 75.9% where S2's shareholder table shows 75.0% for PT Deli Putra Bangsa and 25% public, and the 19.0% free float is sourced to S0 only.
challenges.answer: The archive contains no exchange notice of special-monitoring-board or notation status, so none is asserted; the 19.0% free float is S0-only and the register figure remains an open evidence gap [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: Q25: section 5 says the bull adds the one thing the base refuses to assume, a higher annual RKAB that lets the owned road run toward its 5.0 Mtpa capacity, and section 4 tells the reader that a buyer treating both extensions as certain would see the Rp3,097 bull case. The engine bull is only +2pp revenue growth and +4pp gross margin: no quota uplift, no second extension. Section 5's own regulatory paragraph says the second extension is worth nothing in our numbers, so the report contradicts itself about what its own bull contains.
challenges.answer: Section 4 and section 5 now state the bull's two actual shocks, +2pp revenue growth and +4pp gross margin in every forecast year, with no quota uplift and no second extension; the thesis bullet, section 1 and the assumptions bull narrative were corrected to match [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Q29: section 4 states rf 7.4%, mature-market ERP 4.2%, country premium 2.5% and unlevered beta 1.00 give a levered 1.11 and COE 13.3%, and builds a 12.5% WACC on it.
